title: Short Stuff: Robert Johnson and the Devil
summary: Short Stuff episode on the legend of Robert Johnson selling his soul to the devil at the crossroads. The hosts cover Johnson's rough childhood and adult life, his death at about age 27 (reportedly poisoned), and the legend's origins. They recount the juke joint story in Robinsonville, Mississippi, where a young Johnson was driven off the stage while playing badly alongside Son House and Willie Brown. They describe his return about a year or three years later with his own seven-string guitar, Eric Clapton's description of his playing, and the crossroads legend, which seems to have originated with Tommy Johnson. They discuss the Coen Brothers film O Brother, Where Art Thou? and Crossroads with Ralph Macchio, and Johnson's devil-themed songs. Stephen Johnson, his grandson, says the devil references were about personal demons and that Johnson's improvement came from practice under Ike Zimmerman.
topics: blues and rock and roll origins

segments.title: Opening banter and the hosts' relationship with the blues
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode and talk about their mixed feelings toward blues music, which they consider the foundation of rock and roll. Josh says they dislike the commercialized, smooth-jazz-like blues played in Atlanta bars.

segments.title: Robert Johnson's life and early death
segments.summary: The hosts describe Johnson's rough childhood with frequent moves, the loss of his father, and abuse by a stepfather. After his wife Virginia and their baby died in childbirth, he drank heavily and sang the blues more. He died at 27, reportedly poisoned by a jealous husband, which places him in the 27 Club.

segments.title: The Robinsonville juke joint and the seven-string guitar
segments.summary: The story goes that a young Johnson tried to play at a juke joint in Robinsonville, Mississippi, where Son House and Willie Brown were playing, and was asked to stop and leave. A year or so later he returned with his own guitar and was suddenly excellent, using a seventh string. Eric Clapton described his playing as sounding like several players at once.

segments.title: Origins of the crossroads devil legend
segments.summary: The hosts explain the legend that Johnson sold his soul at the crossroads for talent and say it probably began with a mistaken identity involving Tommy Johnson. Tommy Johnson's brother described a crossroads ritual with a large black man who tuned the instrument. The hosts mention that the Coen Brothers' film O Brother, Where Art Thou? included a Tommy Johnson character, and they discuss the film Crossroads with Ralph Macchio.

segments.title: Devil references in Johnson's songs and the practice explanation
segments.summary: The hosts note devil-themed song titles such as Hellhound on My Trail and Me and the Devil Blues and say that devil imagery was common in blues. Stephen Johnson, the grandson, says the songs were about personal demons. Stephen Johnson also says Johnson's improvement came from about three years of study under Ike Zimmerman, and that practice explains his skill.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and credit How Stuff Works as the source article.
